I sit on a panel that funds projects between the arts and medicine, and the first thing I read in any application is not the idea. It is the paragraph on limitations. If it is missing, the applicant cannot have thought very hard about the work, or they must be hoping we will not notice. If it is there and it is honest, I relax. The best one I read this year said, more or less: we interviewed twelve families, so this cannot be a claim about the whole city; some of them might have told us what they thought we wanted to hear; and we do not yet know whether the effect lasts beyond six months. Three sentences, three modals, and I trusted everything else in that application more because of them. Admitting what you do not know is not weakness on a panel. It is the clearest sign of rigor we have.

People outside research imagine that a review is a verdict. It is closer to a conversation with somebody who has read your work more carefully than anybody else will. When a reviewer writes that a claim must be overstated, the useful response is not to defend it. It is to ask what evidence would corroborate it, and whether you have that evidence. Sometimes you do, and you simply forgot to include it. Sometimes you do not, and the claim has to become smaller and more honest. In my field, the humanities side of medicine, most of our evidence is anecdotal by design. That is not a flaw we hide. It is a limitation we name, and naming it is what allows the stories to be taken seriously. A report that sounds certain about everything is the one I would trust least.
